Unit 4 concepts · 3 / 53
01 · Image-to-image · a new game
From noise to images, to images
Story so far: Units 1–3 made images from random noise. Now: turn one image into another.
G
Before: Units 1–3
Random numbers in. A brand-new face out.
G
Now: Unit 4
A sketch of a shoe in. A photo of that shoe out.
Many more
Day to night, map to satellite view.
The input is now a real image with shapes and meaning. The output keeps its layout; only the look changes.
Why we need a new game: many useful tasks start from an image we already have.

01 · Image-to-image · examples
What image-to-image can do
Left: the input image · right: the output the GAN makes from it
Black & white → colour
Old photos get their colours.
Day → night
Same street, lit windows.
Face sketch → face
A drawing becomes a realistic face.
Segmentation map → street
Colours mean road, car, sky.
Satellite → map
Fields and roads become a clean map.
Edges → shoe photo
Outline in, product photo out.
Every task: the same scene shown two ways; the GAN learns to go from one to the other.
Why we need this view: one method covers all these tasks; only the training images change.
Unit 4 concepts · 5 / 53
01 · Image-to-image · what is new
Not a regular GAN
G
Regular GAN
In: random noise, no meaning.
Out: a brand-new image.
Learns: what real images look like.
G
Image-to-image GAN
In: a real image, full of shapes.
Out: a changed version of the same image.
Learns: how to go from one kind of image to another.
Domain: one kind of image. For example: all shoe sketches, or all shoe photos.
Mapping: the rule that turns any image of one domain into its match in the other.
Why we need the difference: the goal is no longer “any realistic image” but “the right image for this input”.

01 · Image-to-image · conditional GAN
It is a conditional GAN again
A cGAN (conditional GAN, Unit 2) gets a condition: an instruction that says what to draw.
“7”
and z
G
Unit 2: a label
Condition: “draw a 7”. Plus z (the noise vector).
G
Unit 4: a whole image
Condition: “draw the photo for this sketch”.
No noise needed
The sketch already says what to draw. A little randomness comes later, from dropout.
x: the input image (the sketch) · y: the target image (the real photo of that shoe). In Unit 2, y was a label; now y is a whole image.
Why we need this link: everything we know about conditional GANs still works; only the condition changes.
Unit 4 concepts · 7 / 53
01 · Image-to-image · paired data
Paired data
Every input comes with its own matching target: the sketch of shoe 1 with the photo of shoe 1.
purple link: same shoe · green: real photo
Hard to collect
Someone must make every pair by hand, for the very same shoe.
Easier to learn
For every input, the right answer is given. G can check its output against it.
Pix2Pix learns from paired data: this unit.
Why we need pairs here: a pair tells G exactly which output is right for each input.

Unit 4 concepts · 9 / 53
02 · Encoder-decoder · the idea
An image in, an image out
Story so far: We want G to read an image. Now: a generator that takes an image in.
input image
encoder
bottleneck
decoder
output image
G (the generator)
Encoder: shrinks the image into a small summary.
Decoder: grows the summary into a full image.
Output and input have the same size, so the output can be laid over the target photo.
Why we need an encoder-decoder: G must now read a whole image, not a list of noise numbers.
Unit 4 concepts · 10 / 53
02 · Encoder-decoder · the bottleneck
The bottleneck problem
Everything about the image must pass through the small summary in the middle.
1 · A busy input
Buildings, windows, a car.
2 · Squeezed tight
Many details go in. Only a few fit through.
3 · A blurry output
The layout is right. Edges and windows are smeared.
The decoder knows the layout. It must guess exact edges and windows.
Coming in section 05: U-Net passes the details around the bottleneck.
Why we need to see this: it explains blurry outputs, and why Pix2Pix uses U-Net.
Unit 4 concepts · 11 / 53
03 · Why add a GAN? · pixel matching
Just match the pixels?
Story so far: We can train on pairs. Now: is matching pixels enough?
orange: G’s output · green: the target photo · purple: same spot, compared
1 · The answer is known
Each sketch comes with its real photo.
2 · Compare each pixel
Same spot in output and target: how far apart?
3 · Close the gaps
Training nudges every pixel towards the target.
A pixel-match loss (often called L1 loss): bigger gaps, bigger loss.
It works, partly: the shape is right, but the result looks blurry.
Why we ask this: pixel matching is the obvious first try, and its weakness shows why we add a GAN.
Unit 4 concepts · 12 / 53
03 · Why add a GAN? · the average
Pixel loss averages the answers
Task: colour in a black-and-white photo of a car.
1 · Grey car in
The photo shows no colour at all.
2 · Two right answers
Red cars and blue cars are both real.
3 · G paints the middle
A muddy in-between colour. No real car looks like this.
G cannot know which colour is right. Halfway keeps the pixel gap small either way.
Skies turn greyish, bricks brownish. The result: blurry, washed-out images.
Why we need to see this: a blend of right answers is not itself a right answer.
Unit 4 concepts · 13 / 53
03 · Why add a GAN? · two losses
A GAN loss adds sharpness
dashed purple: the outline of the input sketch · orange frame: G’s output
Pixel loss only
Right shape, in the right place. But blurry.
GAN loss only
Sharp and realistic. But it may invent the wrong shoe.
Both together
Sharp and correct.
GAN loss: D asks “does this look real?” Blurry images fail, so G learns to be sharp.
Pixel loss: “is this close to the target?” Wrong shoes fail, so G stays correct.
Why we need both: each one fixes exactly the other one’s weakness.
Unit 4 concepts · 14 / 53
03 · Why add a GAN? · the new D
D judges the pair
D (the discriminator) now sees the input sketch and the photo together.
D
real
Real pair
Sketch with the real photo of that shoe. D should say “real”.
D
fake
Fake pair
Sketch with G’s shoe. D should say “fake”.
The new question
Not “is this a shoe?”
“Is this the right shoe for this sketch?”
But how does D see two images? They are stacked into one input.
If D saw only the photo, G could draw any nice shoe and ignore the sketch.
Why we need a pair-judging D: it forces G’s output to match its own input.
Unit 4 concepts · 15 / 53
04 · PatchGAN · one score
One score is too coarse
Story so far: D now judges input–output pairs. Now: make D judge every part of the image.
blue bar: the one score a normal D (discriminator) gives for the whole image
All sharp
One score: high → “real”.
Blurry windows
One score: medium → “partly fake”.
Blurry walls
One score: medium → “partly fake”.
Same score, different problems. G (the generator) can’t tell where to fix the image.
Why only one score? D shrinks the image down to one answer.
Why we need more than one score: G must know which part of the image looks fake.
Unit 4 concepts · 16 / 53
04 · PatchGAN · the idea
PatchGAN: a grid of judgements
green patch: looks real · orange patch: looks fake · dashed lines: the patches
G’s image, cut into patches
D
PatchGAN
one judgement per patch
Top and bottom rows: real. Walls and windows are sharp.
Middle row: fake. Right on the blurry windows.
But how? D stops shrinking early: each output cell sees one patch.
Why we need a grid: it shows G exactly where the image fails.
Unit 4 concepts · 17 / 53
04 · PatchGAN · patch size
How big is a patch?
purple square: the area one judgement looks at
Too small: one pixel
Checks colours. Can’t see any shapes.
Too big: whole image
No better result. D gets much bigger.
Medium: Pix2Pix’s choice
Sharp texture. Sensible structure.
Medium patch: about a quarter of the image width. Big enough for a window, small enough for detail.
Found by experiment: the Pix2Pix authors tried several sizes and compared the results.
Why we need the middle size: it gives texture and structure without a huge D.
Unit 4 concepts · 18 / 53
04 · PatchGAN · why it works
Why patches work
Four reasons Pix2Pix uses a PatchGAN as its D (discriminator):
Checks everywhere
Every patch is checked, not just the average.
A texture judge
Asks “do these bricks, leaves, laces look real?”
A smaller D
Fewer weights than a whole-image D.
Any image size
A bigger image just gives a bigger grid.
What patches don’t check: the layout of the whole image. The pixel-match part of the training covers that.
Why we need patches: sharp, real-looking texture in every corner of the image.
Unit 4 concepts · 19 / 53
05 · U-Net · the lost details
The encoder had the details
Story so far: PatchGAN demands sharp detail. Now: give the decoder the details back.
The plain encoder-decoder from before, on the street scene: follow one building through it.
Early encoder layer
Knows exactly where every edge and window is.
The bottleneck
Only a short summary: “a building, some windows”.
Decoder output
Has to guess positions: blurry windows.
The encoder had the details. They were lost on the way, not missing.
The fix: hand the early details straight across to the decoder.
Why we need a fix: PatchGAN punishes blur, but the decoder can’t draw what it never received.
Unit 4 concepts · 20 / 53
05 · U-Net · skip connections
Skip connections: bridges across
sketch in
photo out
ENCODER: shrinks ↓
DECODER: grows ↑
bottleneck
bridge
Before: one path, through the bottleneck.
Bridges: each encoder level sends a copy straight across.
Each bridge joins two levels of the same size.
The drawing is a U. So it is called U-Net.
Why we need skip connections: the decoder gets the exact details straight from the encoder.
Unit 4 concepts · 21 / 53
05 · U-Net · what a bridge carries
What a bridge carries
One decoder level, drawing the shoe: it now receives two things.
From below
The decoder’s own picture. WHAT: a shoe, its shape, its colours.
Across the bridge
The encoder’s copy. WHERE: every edge and lace, exactly.
Stacked together
Placed side by side. The next layer reads both.
Stacked, not mixed: both pictures stay whole, one behind the other.
Why the same size? The two pictures must line up spot by spot.
Why we need both: WHAT alone is blurry, WHERE alone just copies the sketch.
Unit 4 concepts · 22 / 53
05 · U-Net · dropout
Dropout instead of noise
Dropout: in the first three decoder layers, some signals are randomly set to zero on every run.
The risk: copying
U-Net could pass the sketch straight across, barely changed.
Dropout
Randomly switches off half the signals. G must use several paths.
Kept on afterwards
Each run of the trained G gives a slightly different shoe.
It replaces z (the noise vector). Dropout is now G’s source of randomness.
Usually dropout is switched off after training. Pix2Pix keeps it on, on purpose.
Why we need dropout here: it stops pure copying and allows several valid answers.

06 · Pix2Pix · overview
Pix2Pix: all the pieces
Story so far: We have U-Net and PatchGAN. Now: train them together.
orange: G (generator) and its fake · green: real · blue: D (discriminator) · purple: pixel-match
sketch (input)
G
U-Net
G’s fake photo
real photo (target)
pixel-match
fake pair
real pair
D
PatchGAN
judges each pair, patch by patch
Pix2Pix (Isola et al., 2017): G is a U-Net, D is a PatchGAN.
Trained on pairs: every sketch comes with its real photo.
Why we need every piece: D gives sharpness, pixel-match gives correctness, U-Net keeps the details.
Unit 4 concepts · 24 / 53
06 · Pix2Pix · G’s goals
G’s two goals
After every sketch, G (the generator) gets feedback from two places at once.
Goal 1 · fool D
Look real to D (the discriminator). Gives sharp textures.
Goal 2 · match the photo
Stay close to the real photo. Gives the correct shape and colours.
How much each counts: correct first, then sharp
match the photo
counts far more
fool D
the finishing touch
Why we need two goals: matching alone is blurry, fooling D alone can be wrong.
Unit 4 concepts · 25 / 53
06 · Pix2Pix · the balance
Getting the balance right
purple slider: how strongly G (the generator) must match the real photo
No pixel-match
A beautiful shoe that ignores the sketch.
Pixel-match far too strong
The right shoe, but soft and blurry.
The Pix2Pix balance
Sharp and correct. The shoe in the sketch.
Found by experiment: the authors tried settings and kept the one that looked best.
The same balance works well across many image-to-image tasks.
Why we need the balance: too little matching gives wrong shoes, too much gives blurry ones.
Unit 4 concepts · 26 / 53
06 · Pix2Pix · augmentation
Change both images the same way
Random crop and flip give more training variety from the same pairs.
The pair
Sketch and photo line up exactly.
Wrong: changed separately
Different crop, different flip. The pair no longer matches.
Right: changed together
Same crop, same flip. Still a matching pair.
In practice: enlarge both a little, cut the same square from both, then flip both or neither.
If they don’t match: G is taught the wrong answer for that sketch.
Why we need the same change: the photo must stay the right answer for its sketch.
Unit 4 concepts · 27 / 53
06 · Pix2Pix · why it works
Three forces, all needed
Why Pix2Pix works: three parts, each doing one job.
Pixel-match
Structure and colour. Without it: G ignores the sketch.
GAN loss (fool D)
Sharp textures. Without it: blurry photos.
U-Net bridges
Exact positions. Without them: details lost.
Remove any one: quality drops clearly.
Each one covers a weakness of the other two.
Why we need all three: sharp, correct and detailed only happen together.
Unit 4 concepts · 28 / 53
06 · Pix2Pix · recipe
The Pix2Pix recipe in words
The parts
1
G (generator): a U-Net with bridges and dropout.
2
D (discriminator): a PatchGAN that sees the pair.
3
Data: sketch–photo pairs, same crop and flip for both.
Training, round after round
4
D’s turn: judge one real pair and one fake pair.
5
G’s turn: fool D and match the real photo.
6
Repeat: one pair at a time, many passes over all the data.
Afterwards: dropout stays on. Each run gives a slightly different photo.
Optimiser: Adam, as in Unit 1’s GANs.
Why we need the recipe: every piece of this unit, in the order you would build it.

07 · Beyond images · the framework
One recipe, many tasks
Story so far: Pix2Pix works for shoes. Now: how far does the idea stretch?
Three parts · orange: G’s output · green: real target · blue: D
sketch → G → photo
1 · Conditional G
G (the generator) turns the input into an output image.
input + output → D
2 · D judges the pair
D (the discriminator) sees both together: right output for this input?
G’s photo vs the real photo
3 · Match the target
G’s output must stay close to the real target image.
Only the training pairs change: edges → shoes · labels → street · day → night · black & white → colour · low → high resolution
Why we need the framework: one design serves many tasks; for a new task we collect new pairs.
Unit 4 concepts · 30 / 53
07 · Beyond images · extensions
Extensions of the framework
Pix2Pix has limits. Each extension keeps the three parts and removes one limit.
No pairs
Learn from two separate collections. CycleGAN, Unit 5.
Higher resolution
First a small rough image. A bigger G adds fine detail.
Many outputs
Add a noise or style code. One sketch, several colourings.
Video
Translate frame after frame. Keep frames consistent: no flicker.
Generalisation: the input can be any image-shaped condition, the output any image-shaped target. A sketch, a label map, a low-resolution photo, a video frame: the recipe does not care.
Why we need extensions: real tasks often lack pairs, need big images, want variety, or move.
Unit 4 concepts · 31 / 53
07 · Beyond images · other modalities
Beyond images
A modality is a kind of data: images, sound, text, tables, signals over time.
time → · pitch ↑
Sound
Spectrogram: a picture of pitch over time. Translate: one voice → another.
“a red bird” → picture
Text → image
The condition is a sentence. G draws a matching picture.
age · blood pressure · diagnosis
Tables
CTGAN: synthetic patient rows. Keeps the links between columns.
heartbeat signal over time
Time series
TimeGAN: synthetic ECG or stock prices. Keeps the patterns over time.
Text itself (e.g. synthetic medical notes) can also be generated. Today large language models do this better than GANs.
Why we need other modalities: much sensitive or scarce data is sound, text, tables or signals, not photos.

07 · Beyond images · what changes
What changes for a new modality
Moving the framework to new data: keep the idea, change the reading and writing.
Stays the same
G (the generator) makes, D (the discriminator) judges. G is conditioned on the input. D judges input and output together. The two train in turns.
Changes
How the data is represented: picture, sequence or table row. The layers that read it and write it.
Modality
Data looks like
Read by
Image
a grid of pixels
convolutions
Sound
a spectrogram picture
convolutions, as for images
Table
one row of column values
plain fully connected layers
Time series
values in time order
layers that read step by step
Why we need this view: to reuse GANs on new data, we only redesign the input and output layers.
Unit 4 concepts · 33 / 53
08 · Data augmentation · scarce data
Deep learning is data-hungry
Story so far: GANs can make realistic images. Now: use them as a tool, to make training data.
high
low
little data
lots of data
Bar height: how well the model works.
More training data → a better model. Most tasks need thousands of labelled examples.
Medical
A rare disease: very few X-rays. Expert labels are costly.
Self-driving
Accidents are rare. No one crashes cars on purpose.
Fraud
Almost all transactions are normal. Fraud examples are few.
Factories
Defects are rare. Breaking products costs money.
Why we need extra data: the cases we most want to detect are the ones we have fewest of.
Unit 4 concepts · 34 / 53
08 · Data augmentation · the classic way
Classic augmentation
Augmentation: make extra training images from the ones we have. The classic way changes existing images.
original · flip · rotate · recolour
Flip, rotate, crop, recolour
Each change gives a new-looking copy.
no extra training
Simple and free
Fast, well understood. Works well for many tasks.
same image, new view
But not new
A rotated dog is still the same dog. Variety stays low.
No fix for a rare class: flipping a few fraud examples gives more of the same few.
What we really want: a completely new dog that looks real. That is what a GAN can make.
Why we need more than classic tricks: they add new views of old images, not new examples.
Unit 4 concepts · 35 / 53
08 · Data augmentation · the recipe
GAN augmentation in four steps
green: real images · orange: GAN-made (synthetic) images · blue: the model we care about
1 · Train a GAN
on the small real set
2 · Generate
many new images
3 · Mix
real + synthetic in one set
4 · Train the downstream model
on both
Downstream model: the model we actually care about. For example a disease detector, a classifier of X-rays.
How many synthetic images? Try a few amounts, compare on real images. More is not always better: GAN flaws can hurt.
Why we need this recipe: the GAN turns a small real set into a bigger, more varied one.
Unit 4 concepts · 36 / 53
08 · Data augmentation · rare classes
Fix a rare class with a cGAN
Bar height: how many images of each class · green: real · orange: GAN-made
common · common · rare
1 · Unbalanced
The rare class has very few images. The model learns to ignore it.
label “rare class” → G → images
2 · Ask for the rare class
A cGAN (conditional GAN, Unit 2) draws the class you name.
rare class topped up
3 · Balanced
A few real images plus many GAN-made ones. Every class is now well represented.
A plain GAN draws random classes: most new images would be common ones. The label lets us spend all the effort on the rare class.
Why we need the cGAN here: it makes exactly the class we are short of, on demand.
Unit 4 concepts · 37 / 53
08 · Data augmentation · labelled data
Pix2Pix makes labelled data
Medical example: a mask is a drawing that marks where the tumour is. Masks are cheap to draw; real scans are expensive.
organ outline + tumour spot
1 · Draw masks
Cheap: a program draws many.
mask → Pix2Pix
2 · Pix2Pix draws scans
Trained first on real mask–scan pairs. Each new mask → a realistic scan.
scan + its mask
3 · Label for free
The mask is the correct label. We know exactly where the tumour is.
Downstream: a tumour-outlining model learns from the new pairs. No expert had to label them.
Why we need this trick: labels are the expensive part, and here they come for free.
Unit 4 concepts · 38 / 53
08 · Data augmentation · when it works
When it helps, when it doesn’t
GAN-made data is not always a win. It depends on how much real data you have, and how good the GAN is.
helps a lot
Small datasets. Rare classes. Rare events. Need variety, not copies.
helps a little
Medium datasets: classic tricks may do. A poor GAN: bad images in, bad model out.
no help
Huge datasets. Tasks needing exact real detail. Data the GAN cannot learn well.
Study (Frid-Adar et al., 2018): liver lesions on CT scans. GAN-made lesions beat classic tricks alone.
Too few images (a few dozen): the GAN memorises. Its “new” images are copies.
Why it matters: GAN augmentation pays off where data is small or rare, not everywhere.
Unit 4 concepts · 39 / 53
08 · Data augmentation · rules and risks
Rules and risks
Rule 1 · Keep the test set clean
Train the GAN on the training images only. Test the model on real images the GAN never saw.
Rule 2 · No new facts
A GAN only remixes what its data contains. It cannot add knowledge that was never there.
Risk · Memorising
The GAN copies real images. Copies add nothing new.
Risk · Mode collapse
Only a few kinds of image (Unit 3). More images, no more variety.
Risk · GAN artefacts
The classifier learns GAN flaws. It then fails on real images.
Check before use: FID (Fréchet Inception distance, Unit 3) for quality, and look at the images. Throw away images with obvious flaws.
Why we need these rules: without them, synthetic data can make a model look better than it is.
Unit 4 concepts · 40 / 53
09 · Privacy and anonymity · the problem
Can a hospital share its X-rays?
Story so far: GANs can make extra data. Now: can they protect privacy?
Hospital A
thousands of patient X-rays
Hospital B
wants to train a diagnosis model
The law
HIPAA (US health-privacy law), GDPR (EU data-protection law). They limit sharing patient data.
Re-identification
An X-ray can be traced back to its patient. Even “anonymised” data often can.
Trust
Hospitals have a duty to their patients.
Idea: Hospital A trains a GAN on its X-rays. It shares synthetic X-rays that look real but belong to no real patient.
Why we need synthetic data: it could let data be shared without exposing real patients.
Unit 4 concepts · 41 / 53
09 · Privacy and anonymity · anonymity
Anonymity: hide who is in the image
Anonymity: no one can tell which person is in the data. Example: street or hospital photos that show people’s faces.
tilted head · smiling
Real photo
Useful for training. But the person can be recognised.
face blurred
Blur it
Private, yes. But no face is left to learn from.
new face · same tilt · same smile
GAN face
A realistic face of nobody. Pose and expression are kept.
How: cut out the real face and keep the scene and the pose. A conditional G draws a new face that fits them.
Why we need GAN anonymisation: the data stays useful, but no person can be recognised.
Unit 4 concepts · 42 / 53
09 · Privacy and anonymity · the risk
Synthetic is not automatically private
Back to the hospital’s GAN · green: real patients · orange: synthetic images
many patients · one rare case
1 · Trained on real patients
Rare cases appear only once or twice.
real rare case → near-copy
2 · It memorises
The GAN may reproduce a real patient almost exactly.
“That’s Mrs Johnson!”
3 · Someone recognises her
Privacy is broken, even though the image is “synthetic”.
Rare cases are most at risk: few examples, so the GAN copies them most closely.
Why it matters: synthetic data needs extra protection before it is truly private.
Unit 4 concepts · 43 / 53
09 · Privacy and anonymity · an attack
The membership attack
The attacker has the GAN (or its images) and a photo of a target person. The question: “was this person’s photo used in training?”
many fakes · one near-copy of the target
Way 1 · Search the outputs
Generate many images. Look for one very close to the target.
z → G → the target photo?
Way 2 · GAN inversion
Search for a z (noise vector) that recreates the photo (Unit 3).
“She was in the dataset”
Success
The attacker learns the person was in the training data.
Why that hurts: being in a hospital’s dataset reveals a hospital visit. It may even reveal the diagnosis.
Why we need to know this attack: it shows exactly what a privacy method must block.
Unit 4 concepts · 44 / 53
09 · Privacy and anonymity · differential privacy
Differential privacy: the promise
Same hospital, two training sets that differ in one patient: Mrs Johnson.
all patients + Mrs Johnson
World A · with her
Train a GAN. Look at its images.
same patients, she is left out
World B · without her
Train a GAN. Look at its images.
A and B look alike
The promise
The images are almost the same in both worlds.
So the images reveal almost nothing about her. Or about any one person: a membership attack fails.
Privacy budget ε (epsilon): how much one person may change the output. Smaller ε: more private.
Why we need differential privacy: it is a proven guarantee, not a hope that the GAN didn’t copy.
Unit 4 concepts · 45 / 53
09 · Privacy and anonymity · DP-SGD
DP-SGD in two steps
DP-SGD (differentially private stochastic gradient descent): change how D learns from each batch. Each arrow: one real image’s push on D’s weights (its gradient).
one unusual image pushes hard
Normal training
One rare patient can steer D a lot. D then remembers her.
dashed line: the size limit
Step 1 · Clip
Cut every push down to a size limit. No one image can push hard.
the combined push · plus random noise
Step 2 · Add noise
Add random noise to the combined push. It hides what each image added.
Only D sees real data, so only D needs DP-SGD. G (the generator) learns only through D, so G is protected too.
Why we need both steps: clipping limits each person’s signal; noise hides what is left.

09 · Privacy and anonymity · the trade-off
Privacy versus quality
The privacy budget ε (epsilon) sets how much noise DP-SGD adds · same shoe GAN, three settings
big budget · little noise
Weak privacy
Sharp, realistic images. Little protection.
middle budget
A balance
Good enough images. Useful protection.
small budget · lots of noise
Strong privacy
Blurry, poor images. Strong protection.
Why not both? The noise that hides each person also hides the patterns G must learn.
You choose the balance for each use. Privacy needed too strict for useful images: a private GAN is the wrong tool.
Why it matters: every private GAN pays for privacy with some image quality.
Unit 4 concepts · 47 / 53
09 · Privacy and anonymity · PATE-GAN
PATE-GAN: teachers vote
PATE (Private Aggregation of Teacher Ensembles): another route to differential privacy · blue: judges · orange: G
1 · Split
real data into several parts
2 · Teachers vote
one judge per part: real or fake?
3 · Count with noise
random noise added to the votes
4 · Student judge
learns from the noisy votes
5 · G
trains against the student
The teachers vote on G’s images. The student and G never touch real data.
Privacy is paid only on the noisy votes. In the paper: better images than a DP-SGD GAN at the same budget (Jordon, Yoon & van der Schaar, 2019).
Why we need PATE-GAN: it protects privacy while losing less quality.

09 · Privacy and anonymity · checklist
Before sharing synthetic data
Check
How
Trained with privacy protection
DP-SGD or PATE-GAN, with a chosen budget
Quality checked
FID (Fréchet Inception distance) and looking
No memorised copies
compare each image with its nearest real image
Still useful
train the real task on it and test on real data
Limits written down
state the privacy promise and its limits
Reviewed
the privacy team approves
Worth it for: medical, financial and personal data. Publishing a dataset, or sharing between organisations.
Not worth it for: data that isn’t sensitive. Or when training at each site without moving the data (federated learning) fits better.
Why we need a checklist: one missed step can leak a real person.

10 · Wrap-up · ten ideas
Ten ideas to remember
GANs that transform images
1
Image-to-image is a cGAN whose condition is a whole image.
2
Pixel-matching alone averages the answers: blur.
3
D judges the pair, so G must follow the input.
4
PatchGAN judges every patch: sharp texture everywhere.
5
U-Net bridges hand exact positions to the decoder.
GANs as a tool
6
The same framework stretches to sound, text, tables, time series.
7
GAN-made data helps most when real data is small or rare.
8
Test on real images the GAN never saw.
9
Synthetic is not automatically private: GANs can memorise.
10
DP-SGD: clip each push, add noise; more privacy, lower quality.
Why it matters: these ten lines are the whole unit in short.
Unit 4 concepts · 51 / 53
10 · Wrap-up · check yourself
Explain in one sentence
Why does pixel loss alone blur?
It averages all the right answers into a muddy middle.
Why does D see the input too?
Otherwise G could draw any nice image and ignore the input.
Why does U-Net need bridges?
The bottleneck loses exact positions; bridges carry them across.
Why crop both images the same way?
A different crop breaks the pair: input and target no longer match.
Why isn’t synthetic data automatically private?
The GAN can memorise and reproduce real people, especially rare cases.
What does GAN anonymisation keep and remove?
It keeps pose, expression and scene; it removes who the person is.
Why it matters: if you can say each answer in one sentence, you understand the idea.
